sla_name: Oral conversations in advanced settings
sla_assessment_criteria: Oral conversations are made in different settings accordingly.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Advanced settings are formal and specialised situations such as airports, immigration offices and diplomatic events where precise spoken English is needed.
sla_notes_details: Learners study functional language for check-in, security and migration (May I see your passport? What is the purpose of your visit?), and diplomatic protocol (forms of address such as Your Excellency, order of speaking, courtesy and neutrality). They practise polite requests, formal greetings, indirect questions and clarifying statements, using role plays.
sla_notes_illustrations: At an immigration desk: Officer: How long do you intend to stay? Visitor: I plan to stay for two weeks for a conference.
sla_notes_daily_life: These skills prepare students for careers in tourism, aviation, foreign affairs and international organisations.
sla_exercise: How do you address an ambassador formally?::Your Excellency.||Give a polite question asked at an immigration desk.::What is the purpose of your visit?||Why is indirect language used in diplomacy?::It is more polite and avoids offence.||Name one feature of diplomatic protocol.::Formal address or order of speaking.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the advanced English language skills
specific_competence_name: Automate the production of oral descriptions and conversations using standard pronunciation
learning_activity_name: Narrate documentaries of events, and situations with a standard pronunciation in different contexts (e.g., history, religion and, medicine)
sla_name: Narrating documentaries of events and situations
sla_assessment_criteria: Documentaries of events and situations in different contexts are narrated appropriately with a standard pronunciation.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A documentary narration is a spoken factual account of events or situations, often accompanying images.
sla_notes_details: Learners plan the script (introduction, chronological or thematic development, conclusion), use the past tense for history and the present tense for immediacy, and use suitable vocabulary for fields such as history, religion and medicine. They practise clear pronunciation, steady pace, pauses and tone that suit the subject, and record and review their narration.
sla_notes_illustrations: A narration on the Maji Maji uprising may begin: In 1905, in the southern regions of German East Africa, people rose against forced cotton growing.
sla_notes_daily_life: Narration skills are used in radio, television, tourism guiding and museums.
sla_exercise: Which tense is often used in historical narration?::The simple past.||Name the parts of a narration script.::Introduction, body and conclusion.||Why are pauses important?::They give emphasis and time to absorb information.||Name a field in which documentaries are made.::History, religion or medicine.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the advanced English language skills
specific_competence_name: Automate the production of oral descriptions and conversations using standard pronunciation
learning_activity_name: Participate in dialogues, debates and meetings on topical and cross-cutting issues (e.g. debate, meeting, and presentations) with a standard pronunciation
sla_name: Dialogues, debates and meetings on topical issues
sla_assessment_criteria: Dialogues, debates and meetings are conducted effectively on topical and cross-cutting issues with a standard pronunciation.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Dialogues, debates and meetings are structured speaking events used to exchange and defend ideas.
sla_notes_details: In a debate there is a motion, proposers and opposers, a speaker, timed speeches, rebuttals and points of information. A meeting has an agenda, chairperson, minutes and resolutions. Learners use formal expressions such as: I beg to propose, Point of order, I second the motion, and discuss cross-cutting issues such as environment, human rights and digital literacy.
sla_notes_illustrations: Motion: This house believes that plastic bags should be banned. The proposer argues that plastic pollutes the environment, and the opposer replies that a ban harms small traders.
sla_notes_daily_life: These skills are applied in school parliaments, clubs, board meetings and public forums.
sla_exercise: What is a motion in a debate?::The statement or proposal being debated.||What are minutes of a meeting?::The written record of what was discussed and decided.||What does a rebuttal do?::It answers or challenges the opponent's argument.||Give an expression for supporting a motion.::I second the motion.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the advanced English language skills
specific_competence_name: Use correct grammar and vocabulary in oral and written language tasks
learning_activity_name: Use advanced vocabulary and grammar (e.g., adverbs, prepositions and conjunctions) to describe field specific past, present and future events
sla_name: Advanced grammar to describe field-specific events
sla_method: TIPS, Project work and Group discussions
sla_assessment_criteria: Documentaries of events and situations in different contexts are narrated appropriately with a standard pronunciation.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Advanced grammar such as adverbs, prepositions and conjunctions links ideas precisely in describing past, present and future events in specific fields.
sla_notes_details: Learners use adverbs of manner, degree and frequency, complex prepositional phrases (in accordance with, with regard to), and conjunctions and connectors (although, whereas, consequently, nevertheless). They use appropriate tenses to describe past events (in law or history), present processes (in science) and future plans (in business), and the passive voice for formal reports.
sla_notes_illustrations: The samples were heated slowly; consequently, the solution changed colour. (passive voice and connector in a science report).
sla_notes_daily_life: Accurate use of advanced grammar matters in professional reports, proposals and academic writing.
sla_exercise: Give two conjunctions showing contrast.::Although and whereas (or however, nevertheless).||Change to passive: The lab technician heated the samples.::The samples were heated by the lab technician.||What does the connector consequently show?::Result.||Give a prepositional phrase used in formal writing.::In accordance with.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the advanced English language skills
specific_competence_name: Use correct grammar and vocabulary in oral and written language tasks
learning_activity_name: Compose field specific texts using advanced vocabulary and grammar (e.g., therein, thereof, besides, in addition, although, and however) in different contexts
sla_name: Composing field-specific texts with advanced vocabulary and grammar
sla_assessment_criteria: Field specific texts are composed using appropriate grammar and vocabulary.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Field-specific texts use the vocabulary and structures of a particular profession such as law, medicine, business or engineering.
sla_notes_details: Formal linking words such as therein, thereof, hereby, besides, in addition, although and however are used. Learners write texts such as memoranda, agreements, clinical notes, business proposals and technical descriptions with the correct format. They apply precise terminology, concise sentences and an impersonal tone and check for coherence and accuracy.
sla_notes_illustrations: The tenant shall pay the rent monthly and any damages thereof shall be borne by the tenant (legal English).
sla_notes_daily_life: The skill is used in workplaces, legal drafting and professional communication.
sla_exercise: What does thereof mean?::Of that or of it.||Write one linking word that shows addition.::Besides or in addition.||Why is an impersonal tone used in technical texts?::To keep the writing objective and formal.||Name one document type in the field of law.::A contract, will or affidavit.

main_competence_name: Demonstrate mastery of the advanced English language skills
specific_competence_name: Use correct grammar and vocabulary in oral and written language tasks
learning_activity_name: Evaluate the appropriateness of grammar and vocabulary used in speech and written texts in field specific contexts
sla_name: Evaluating appropriateness of grammar and vocabulary in field-specific contexts
sla_assessment_criteria: Usage of grammar and vocabulary in speech and written the texts of field specific context is evaluated accordingly.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Evaluating means judging whether the language used suits the purpose, audience and field of a text.
sla_notes_details: Learners use criteria: accuracy of grammar, suitability of register, precision of terminology, clarity, conciseness and tone. They compare texts such as a medical report and a social media post, and identify inappropriate slang, ambiguity, wordiness, redundancy or misuse of terms, and suggest corrections.
sla_notes_illustrations: The sentence: The patient is kind of sick is inappropriate in a clinical report and should be: The patient presents with symptoms of illness.
sla_notes_daily_life: The skill helps workers to write and check professional documents.
sla_exercise: Why is slang inappropriate in a legal document?::Legal texts require formal and precise language.||Name two criteria for evaluating language.::Accuracy and appropriateness.||Give an example of redundancy.::Return back (return already implies back).||What is ambiguity?::A statement that can be understood in more than one way.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate advanced oral and written proficiency in a variety of communicative contexts
learning_activity_name: Participate in complex conversations (e.g., death, violence, discrimination, accidents and poor results)
sla_name: Complex conversations on sensitive issues
sla_assessment_criteria: Formal conversations in more complex settings are made accordingly.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Complex conversations deal with sensitive topics such as death, violence, discrimination, accidents and poor results, requiring tact and empathy.
sla_notes_details: Learners use empathetic language (I am sorry for your loss), euphemisms (passed away), softeners (I am afraid that...), careful listening, calm tone and non-judgemental wording. They practise breaking bad news, consoling, reporting a crime and counselling a student with poor results.
sla_notes_illustrations: A teacher tells a student: I am afraid your results are below expectation, but we can plan how to improve them together.
sla_notes_daily_life: These skills are essential for counsellors, teachers, health workers and community leaders.
sla_exercise: What is a euphemism?::A gentle word used in place of a harsh one, e.g. passed away.||Give one empathetic expression.::I am sorry for your loss.||Why is a calm tone important?::It shows respect and reduces distress.||Suggest a softener before bad news.::I am afraid that...

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate advanced oral and written proficiency in a variety of communicative contexts
learning_activity_name: Respond to conversations using rhetorical devices
sla_name: Responding to conversations using rhetorical devices
sla_method: Debate, dialogues, Role-plays and Story- telling
sla_assessment_criteria: Rhetorical devices are used in conversations of different settings correctly to convey meanings.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Rhetorical devices are language techniques that make speech persuasive and memorable.
sla_notes_details: Devices include rhetorical questions, repetition, parallelism, the rule of three, analogy, hyperbole, anecdote, antithesis and appeals to logic (logos), emotion (pathos) and credibility (ethos). Learners identify them in speeches and use them to respond in debates and discussions.
sla_notes_illustrations: I have a dream, repeated in a famous speech, is an example of anaphora. Ask not what your country can do for you is antithesis.
sla_notes_daily_life: Rhetorical skills help in advocacy, marketing and leadership.
sla_exercise: Define repetition as a rhetorical device.::Saying a word or phrase repeatedly for emphasis.||What is ethos?::An appeal based on the speaker's credibility.||What is an analogy?::A comparison to explain an idea.||Give an example of the rule of three.::Government of the people, by the people, for the people.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Demonstrate advanced oral and written proficiency in a variety of communicative contexts
learning_activity_name: Employ paralinguistic features to communicate information in a variety of settings
sla_name: Paralinguistic features in communication
sla_assessment_criteria: Paralinguistic features are employed in communicating information in a variety of settings.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Paralinguistic features are the non-word elements of communication that accompany speech.
sla_notes_details: They include tone of voice, volume, pitch, pace, pauses, laughter, sighs, gestures, facial expressions, posture, eye contact and proximity. Their meaning varies with culture and setting, and they may reinforce, contradict or replace words. Learners practise using them in interviews, presentations and counselling.
sla_notes_illustrations: Saying Fine in a low voice with a frown contradicts the word and shows unhappiness.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding paralinguistic cues helps in negotiation, teaching and customer relations.
sla_exercise: Name two paralinguistic features.::Gestures and tone of voice.||How can body language contradict words?::A speaker may say yes while shaking the head.||Why do meanings of gestures differ?::Because cultures differ.||What is proximity?::The distance between speakers.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Read texts critically to recognise potential implications beyond the author’s explicit meaning
learning_activity_name: Read a variety of texts and identifying the contextual clues (e.g., general context, co-text, punctuations) for understanding implied meanings
sla_name: Contextual clues for implied meaning
sla_assessment_criteria: Contextual clues are recognised and used to understanding implied meanings of texts.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Contextual clues are hints in and around a text that help readers infer the meaning that the author does not state directly.
sla_notes_details: General context refers to the situation, purpose and cultural background; co-text refers to the surrounding words and sentences; punctuation marks such as quotation marks, dashes and exclamation marks suggest tone, irony or emphasis. Readers also use headings, images and the writer's style to draw inferences.
sla_notes_illustrations: In: The so-called expert failed to answer any question, the phrase so-called signals that the writer doubts the person's expertise.
sla_notes_daily_life: The skill helps in reading newspapers, contracts and social media critically.
sla_exercise: What is co-text?::The words and sentences around a word or phrase.||What can quotation marks around a word suggest?::Irony or doubt.||What does an exclamation mark show?::Strong feeling or emphasis.||Define inference.::A conclusion reached from evidence and reasoning.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Read texts critically to recognise potential implications beyond the author’s explicit meaning
learning_activity_name: Read a variety of texts (e.g., letters, articles and newspapers) to obtain implied meanings
sla_name: Reading letters, articles and newspapers for implied meanings
sla_method: Close reading, TIPS and Group works
sla_assessment_criteria: Various texts are red and implied meanings are recognised.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Different text types imply meanings through structure, choice of words and tone.
sla_notes_details: Learners read business and personal letters, feature articles and editorials to identify implied attitudes, bias, hidden requests and persuasive intentions. They examine headlines, word choice (regime versus government), omitted information and the placement of stories, and ask who wrote the text, for whom and why.
sla_notes_illustrations: The headline Youth Idle as Jobs Vanish implies that unemployment is high and criticises the authorities without stating so.
sla_notes_daily_life: Reading between the lines helps citizens to judge news and avoid manipulation.
sla_exercise: What is bias?::A one-sided view.||Give two questions to ask when reading critically.::Who wrote it and why?||How can word choice reveal attitude?::Positive or negative words show the writer's opinion.||What is an editorial?::An article expressing the opinion of the newspaper.

main_competence_name: Comprehend oral and written information
specific_competence_name: Read texts critically to recognise potential implications beyond the author’s explicit meaning
learning_activity_name: Read a variety of texts and comment on the implied meanings from the author’s point of view
sla_name: Commenting on implied meanings from the author's point of view
sla_method: Close reading, TIPS and Group works
sla_assessment_criteria: Various texts are red and appropriate comments on the implied meanings are given.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The author's point of view is the position or attitude from which a text is written.
sla_notes_details: Learners identify the author's purpose (to inform, persuade, entertain), stance, tone (serious, humorous, critical, sympathetic) and assumptions, and discuss how these shape the implied meaning. They write short comments supported by textual evidence and consider whether the author is objective or biased.
sla_notes_illustrations: An article that describes street vendors as hard-working entrepreneurs, rather than illegal traders, shows a sympathetic point of view.
sla_notes_daily_life: The skill is useful in literature study, media literacy and research.
sla_exercise: What is tone?::The author's attitude towards the subject.||Give two purposes of an author.::To inform and to persuade.||How do you support a comment on point of view?::With evidence from the text.||What is an objective text?::A text presenting facts without personal feelings.

main_competence_name: Communicate effectively in different contexts
specific_competence_name: Develop advanced socio-cultural analysis of functional texts
learning_activity_name: Assess the appropriateness of the language and style used in functional texts
sla_name: Language and style in functional texts
sla_assessment_criteria: Language usage and style in the functional texts are analysed and evaluated.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Functional texts are written for practical purposes, such as letters, notices, minutes, reports, advertisements and instructions.
sla_notes_details: Learners assess whether the language and style suit the purpose, audience and culture: level of formality, politeness, directness, vocabulary, layout and length. They consider socio-cultural appropriateness, for example how requests, refusals and greetings are expressed in different cultures, and rewrite inappropriate parts.
sla_notes_illustrations: A letter to a chief may begin with respectful greetings before making a request, showing awareness of cultural politeness.
sla_notes_daily_life: The assessment skill helps in writing official letters, advertisements and public notices.
sla_exercise: What is a functional text?::A text used to perform a practical task.||Give two examples of functional texts.::A notice and a letter of application.||What does audience determine?::The language, tone and level of formality.||Why is cultural appropriateness important?::To avoid offence and communicate effectively.

main_competence_name: Communicate effectively in different contexts
specific_competence_name: Develop advanced socio-cultural analysis of functional texts
learning_activity_name: Differentiate the structure and style of different functional texts
sla_name: Structure and style of different functional texts
sla_method: RIPS, Project work, TIPS and Group discussions
sla_assessment_criteria: Evidence based on structure and style of functional texts are used to support the differentiation.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Each functional text has a typical structure and style.
sla_notes_details: A formal letter has sender address, date, receiver address, salutation, subject line, body, closing and signature. A report has title, introduction, findings, conclusion and recommendations. Minutes have heading, attendance, agenda items, resolutions and signature. An advertisement uses catchy headings, persuasive language and contact details. A notice is short and clear, giving what, when, where and who. Learners compare the texts.
sla_notes_illustrations: Minutes are written in the past tense and reported speech, e.g. It was resolved that the school fees be reviewed.
sla_notes_daily_life: Knowing the structures helps learners to prepare documents at school and at work.
sla_exercise: Name two parts of a formal letter.::Salutation and subject line.||Which tense is used in minutes?::The past tense.||What does a notice give?::What, when, where and who.||What language feature marks advertisements?::Persuasive and catchy wording.

main_competence_name: Provide advanced English language services to the community
specific_competence_name: Apply principles of interpretation to provide complex and authentic interpretations
learning_activity_name: Interpret conversations in field specific settings (e.g., legal, medicine, religion, science and technology)
sla_name: Interpreting field-specific conversations
sla_assessment_criteria: Conversations in field specific settings are interpreted.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Field-specific interpretation takes place in specialised settings such as legal, medical, religious, and scientific and technological contexts.
sla_notes_details: Interpreters prepare by studying glossaries and background of the field. In legal settings (courts, police stations) accuracy and impartiality are vital and terms like bail, testimony and oath are rendered exactly. In medicine, they interpret symptoms and instructions and respect patient privacy. In religion, they interpret sermons faithfully, and in science and technology they convey technical terms and processes.
sla_notes_illustrations: A court interpreter renders the witness's answer word for word, without adding explanations, so that the judge hears the exact testimony.
sla_notes_daily_life: The skill provides careers in courts, hospitals and international conferences.
sla_exercise: Why must court interpretation be exact?::Because it affects the judgement and the rights of people.||How do interpreters prepare for a specialised assignment?::By studying glossaries and background information.||Name one medical ethical requirement.::Patient confidentiality.||What does testimony mean?::A statement made by a witness in court.

main_competence_name: Provide advanced English language services to the community
specific_competence_name: Apply principles of interpretation to provide complex and authentic interpretations
learning_activity_name: Solve the challenges that may arise when interpreting field specific conversations
sla_name: Solving challenges in interpreting field-specific conversations
sla_assessment_criteria: Challenges of interpretations in field specific conversations are solved.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Interpreters face challenges such as unfamiliar terms, speed, accents, emotional situations and cultural differences.
sla_notes_details: Solutions include preparation and glossaries, asking speakers to slow down or repeat, using note-taking, paraphrasing terms that have no equivalent, working in teams, taking breaks, keeping a professional emotional distance and clarifying cultural references briefly. Interpreters should be honest about any term they cannot render and check it.
sla_notes_illustrations: If a speaker uses a technical term that has no Kiswahili equivalent, the interpreter may borrow the term and add a short explanation.
sla_notes_daily_life: Solving these challenges improves the quality of service in hospitals, courts and businesses.
sla_exercise: Name two challenges of interpreting.::Speed and unfamiliar terminology.||How can an interpreter handle a term with no equivalent?::By borrowing it or paraphrasing it.||What is one way to reduce fatigue?::Working in teams and taking breaks.||Why is preparation important?::It equips the interpreter with terms and background.

main_competence_name: Provide advanced English language services to the community
specific_competence_name: Apply principles of translation to produce complex authentic translation
learning_activity_name: Translate a variety of complex technical texts using Computer-Assisted Translation (CAT) tools
sla_name: Translating technical texts using CAT tools
sla_assessment_criteria: Complex technical texts are translated using computer assisted translation tools.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Technical texts contain specialised terminology and require accuracy, for example manuals, scientific papers, legal contracts and medical leaflets.
sla_notes_details: The translator sets up a project in a CAT tool, imports translation memories and terminology databases, translates segment by segment, uses concordance search to check terms, runs spell-check and quality assurance, and exports the file in its original format. Consistency of terms and formatting is vital, and human review remains necessary.
sla_notes_illustrations: Translating a user manual for a machine, the tool suggests previous translations of the term circuit breaker so that the same equivalent is used throughout.
sla_notes_daily_life: Technical translation is a growing career for companies, engineers and international organisations.
sla_exercise: What is concordance search?::A search that shows how a term was translated in previous texts.||Why is consistency important in technical translation?::It avoids confusion and errors.||What kinds of text are technical texts?::Manuals, scientific papers and legal contracts.||Why is human review still necessary?::Software cannot fully judge context and meaning.

main_competence_name: Provide advanced English language services to the community
specific_competence_name: Apply principles of translation to produce complex authentic translation
learning_activity_name: Address challenges that may arise during translation of technical texts
sla_name: Challenges in translating technical texts
sla_assessment_criteria: Challenges that arise during translation of technical texts are solved.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Technical translation faces challenges of terminology, culture, format and technology.
sla_notes_details: Challenges include lack of equivalent terms, ambiguous source text, differing units and conventions (dates and measures), inconsistent terminology, tight deadlines, confidentiality and poor machine output. Solutions include research using dictionaries and subject experts, glossary creation, creating neologisms carefully, consulting the client and revising the work.
sla_notes_illustrations: The term cloud computing may have no established Kiswahili term, so the translator may keep the English term with an explanatory note, or coin an agreed equivalent.
sla_notes_daily_life: Addressing these challenges ensures reliable translations for health, technology and trade.
sla_exercise: Give one challenge in technical translation.::Lack of equivalent terms.||Who can help a translator with specialised terms?::Subject experts or the client.||What is a neologism?::A newly created word.||Why should translators check units and dates?::Conventions differ between languages and regions.

main_competence_name: Provide advanced English language services to the community
specific_competence_name: Apply principles of editing and proofreading a variety of texts
learning_activity_name: Edit and proofread complex field specific texts
sla_name: Editing and proofreading complex field-specific texts
sla_method: Project work, TIPS and Group discussion
sla_assessment_criteria: Complex field specific texts are edited and proofread.
sla_teaching_aids: Field specific texts e.g|Legal texts|Professional reports|Dissertations
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Field-specific texts such as legal, medical, technical and academic documents require editors who understand the field.
sla_notes_details: The editor checks terminology, accuracy of facts and figures, consistency of style, logical flow, tables and references, and the house style. Legal texts require precision, medical texts require correct dosage and terms, and academic texts require correct citation. The editor uses track changes and a checklist and queries the author on doubtful points.
sla_notes_illustrations: In a medical leaflet the editor confirms that the dosage 5 mg has not been mistyped as 50 mg.
sla_notes_daily_life: Careful editing prevents costly or dangerous errors in documents.
sla_exercise: Why must an editor check figures carefully?::A small error can cause serious consequences.||What is track changes?::A feature that shows edits made to a document.||Name one thing checked in academic editing.::Citations and references.||What should an editor do when unsure of an author's meaning?::Query the author.

main_competence_name: Provide advanced English language services to the community
specific_competence_name: Apply principles of editing and proofreading a variety of texts
learning_activity_name: Evaluate edited field specific texts with an editorial perspective
sla_name: Evaluating edited field-specific texts
sla_assessment_criteria: Edited field specific texts are evaluated with an editorial perspective.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Evaluating an edited text means judging its quality from the editor's point of view.
sla_notes_details: The evaluator compares the edited version with the original, using criteria such as accuracy, clarity, consistency, appropriateness of tone, adherence to house style, layout and absence of errors. He also checks that the author's meaning and voice were preserved and gives feedback with constructive suggestions.
sla_notes_illustrations: Comparing two versions of a company report, the evaluator notes that the edited version has consistent headings and removes repetition but has changed the meaning of one paragraph, and recommends restoring it.
sla_notes_daily_life: Evaluation skills are used in publishing houses, media houses and quality control in translation firms.
sla_exercise: Name two criteria for evaluating an edited text.::Accuracy and consistency.||What should be preserved when editing?::The author's meaning and voice.||Why give constructive feedback?::To help improve future work.||What is house style?::The set of writing rules of an organisation.

main_competence_name: Provide advanced English language services to the community
specific_competence_name: Manage complex translation and edit projects using Computer-Assisted tools
learning_activity_name: Explain the qualities of a translation project manager
sla_name: Qualities of a translation project manager
sla_assessment_criteria: The qualities of a translation project manager are explained correctly.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A translation project manager plans, coordinates and delivers translation work for clients.
sla_notes_details: Qualities include organisation, communication, leadership, attention to detail, time management, technical knowledge of CAT tools, knowledge of languages and subject fields, negotiation, problem-solving, integrity and the ability to work under pressure. The manager selects translators and editors, sets deadlines, controls quality and communicates with clients.
sla_notes_illustrations: A manager receiving a 40,000-word contract divides it among four translators, sets a glossary for consistent terms and schedules editing before delivery.
sla_notes_daily_life: Project management skills open careers in translation companies and international institutions.
sla_exercise: Name two qualities of a project manager.::Organisation and communication.||What tasks does the manager perform?::Plans, assigns, monitors and delivers translation work.||Why is a glossary helpful when many translators work on a project?::It keeps terminology consistent.||Why is time management important?::To meet client deadlines.

main_competence_name: Provide advanced English language services to the community
specific_competence_name: Manage complex translation and edit projects using Computer-Assisted tools
learning_activity_name: Use Computer-Assisted Translation (CAT) tools to manage translation projects (e.g., writing quotations, invoices and contracts)
sla_name: Managing translation projects with CAT tools
sla_assessment_criteria: Translation projects are correctly managed using CAT tools.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: CAT tools help project managers to organise workflows, manage files and prepare financial documents.
sla_notes_details: Steps include receiving the client's request, analysing the files (word count, repetitions), preparing a quotation based on rates per word, writing a contract with terms, creating a project in the tool, assigning tasks to translators, monitoring progress, performing quality checks, delivering and invoicing. The quotation should give scope, rate, deadline and payment terms, and the invoice should be clear and correct.
sla_notes_illustrations: For a 10,000-word document at 50 shillings per word the quotation is 500,000 shillings, with a discount for repetitions found by the tool.
sla_notes_daily_life: These skills support self-employment as freelance translators and language service providers.
sla_exercise: What is a quotation?::A document stating the price and terms for a job.||What does an invoice request?::Payment for work done.||Calculate the cost of 8,000 words at 40 shillings per word.::320,000 shillings.||Name one item to include in a contract.::Deadline, payment terms or scope.

main_competence_name: Appreciate and create literary works
specific_competence_name: Evaluate the context in which literary texts are written, read and understood
learning_activity_name: Analyse the settings of literary texts to show their contributions to the content
sla_name: Analysing settings of literary texts
sla_assessment_criteria: Settings of literary texts are analysed to show their contributions to the content.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: The setting is the time, place and social environment in which a literary work takes place.
sla_notes_details: Learners analyse physical setting (village, city, school), historical time, social and cultural background and atmosphere. They show how setting influences the plot, characters and themes, creates mood, and serves symbolic purposes. Answers are supported with descriptive quotations from the text.
sla_notes_illustrations: In a novel set in a colonial farm, the harsh working environment highlights the theme of exploitation.
sla_notes_daily_life: Understanding setting improves reading of novels, films and plays.
sla_exercise: What is setting?::The time and place of a story.||How can setting create mood?::Through descriptions of weather, places and atmosphere.||Give one way setting affects characters.::It shapes their actions and choices.||What is a social setting?::The customs and conditions of the society in the story.

main_competence_name: Appreciate and create literary works
specific_competence_name: Evaluate the context in which literary texts are written, read and understood
learning_activity_name: Relate the content of literary works to real life situations
sla_name: Relating content of literary works to real-life situations
sla_assessment_criteria: Content of literary works is related appropriately to the real-life situations.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Readers link events, characters and issues in a literary work to real happenings in society.
sla_notes_details: Learners identify a situation in the text, such as unemployment, corruption, gender bias, migration or environmental destruction, compare it with real situations in their country and discuss causes, effects and solutions. They write reflective essays and take part in discussions to demonstrate the relevance of literature.
sla_notes_illustrations: A novel about a young person leaving a village for the city relates to real rural-urban migration in Tanzania.
sla_notes_daily_life: Relating literature to life makes reading meaningful and encourages social awareness.
sla_exercise: Why relate literature to real life?::To show its relevance and lessons.||Give one issue often found in literature.::Corruption or migration.||What is a reflective essay?::An essay showing personal thoughts on a text.||Name one skill developed by such relation.::Critical thinking.

main_competence_name: Appreciate and create literary works
specific_competence_name: Evaluate the context in which literary texts are written, read and understood
learning_activity_name: Infer moral lessons from a variety of literary works
sla_name: Inferring moral lessons from literary works
sla_assessment_criteria: Moral lessons from a variety of literary works are appropriately inferred.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A moral lesson is a message about proper behaviour that a reader draws from a text.
sla_notes_details: Readers examine characters' actions, consequences, resolution and the narrator's comments to infer lessons such as honesty, perseverance, respect, justice and responsibility. They distinguish theme from moral and back the inference with evidence. Moral lessons are stated in full sentences.
sla_notes_illustrations: In a fable where a lazy animal starves in the dry season, the moral is that hard work brings security.
sla_notes_daily_life: Moral lessons guide behaviour at home, school and work.
sla_exercise: Difference between a theme and a moral?::A theme is the central idea; a moral is the lesson on behaviour.||Give one moral lesson.::Honesty is the best policy.||How is a moral inferred?::From the actions and consequences of characters.||Where are morals commonly found?::In fables, folktales and novels.

main_competence_name: Appreciate and create literary works
specific_competence_name: Create complex literary works
learning_activity_name: Formulate an idea for composing literary work of literature
sla_name: Formulating an idea for a literary work
sla_assessment_criteria: Ideas for composing literary works are we1ll formulated.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Formulating an idea is the first stage in creative writing, when a writer selects the central concept to be developed.
sla_notes_details: Ideas are drawn from observation, experience, imagination, news, memories and issues in society. The writer asks what is the message, who is the audience, and which genre is suitable. Techniques include brainstorming, free writing, mind maps and what-if questions. The idea is then refined into a central theme statement.
sla_notes_illustrations: Idea: A girl from a poor family fights to stay in school despite pressure to marry. Theme: Education empowers.
sla_notes_daily_life: Generating ideas is a skill for authors, scriptwriters and advertisers.
sla_exercise: Name one source of literary ideas.::Personal experience or news.||What is brainstorming?::Listing ideas freely without judging them.||What is a what-if question?::A question that explores possibilities, e.g. What if the village lost its water?||Why decide on the audience?::It guides language and content.

main_competence_name: Appreciate and create literary works
specific_competence_name: Create complex literary works
learning_activity_name: Develop plans of writing literary works (e.g., characters, themes, setting and plot)
sla_name: Planning literary works
sla_assessment_criteria: Plans of writing literary works are developed correctly.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: A plan gives the writer a framework for characters, themes, setting and plot before writing.
sla_notes_details: Planning includes profiles of characters (name, age, traits, goals), the setting in time and place, the plot outline (exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution), the point of view, the tone and the themes. Writers may use plot diagrams, storyboards or chapter outlines.
sla_notes_illustrations: A plan for a short story lists: Character: Neema, a determined student; Setting: a rural school; Conflict: lack of fees; Climax: a scholarship exam; Resolution: she wins.
sla_notes_daily_life: Planning skills are useful in writing essays, reports and scripts too.
sla_exercise: Name the parts of a plot.::Exposition, rising action, climax, falling action and resolution.||What is a character profile?::A description of a character's traits and background.||Why plan before writing?::It organises ideas and prevents confusion.||What is point of view?::The perspective from which a story is told.

main_competence_name: Appreciate and create literary works
specific_competence_name: Create complex literary works
learning_activity_name: Apply literary skills in developing literary works
sla_name: Applying literary skills in developing literary works
sla_assessment_criteria: Literary skills are used to develop literary works.
sla_references: TET(2023), ENGLISH LANGUAGE SYLLABUS FOR ADVANCED SECONDARY EDUCATION, TET, DAR ES SALAAM
sla_notes_intro: Literary skills are the techniques writers use to craft engaging and meaningful texts.
sla_notes_details: These include showing rather than telling, creating vivid imagery, using dialogue that reveals character, controlling pace, building suspense, using figures of speech, choosing a consistent point of view, and revising drafts. Learners write short stories, poems or scenes, share them for feedback, and edit and publish them in school magazines or online.
sla_notes_illustrations: Instead of writing: He was afraid, a writer shows: His hands trembled and his voice cracked as he stepped into the dark room.
sla_notes_daily_life: Creative writing skills are useful in journalism, advertising, film and education.
sla_exercise: What does show, don't tell mean?::Using actions and details to reveal feelings instead of stating them.||Name one figure of speech a writer may use.::Simile or metaphor.||Why is revision important?::It improves clarity and quality.||How can writers share their work?::Through magazines, blogs or readings.
